Part A · Fairness

A0 · See it update

a0_column <- pick_a_column(fairness)

a0 <- ggplot(fairness, aes(y = .data[[a0_column]])) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "My Favorite Plot", x = "Count", y = a0_column)

show_plot(a0)

WRITE (1 sentence): Did your title change show up here and in your slides?

A1 · Label it

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = ifelse(income >= 50000, "Above 50k", "Below 50k"),
    has_outcome = income >= 50000
  )

a1_base <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(rate = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of total", y = NULL)

a1 <- a1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Over or Under 50k",
    subtitle = "What proportion of NC residents make 50k+",
    x = "Proportion",
    y = NULL,
  )

show_plot(a1)
## heavily changed a1_base and a1 in efforts to get the proper proportions of each group shown

WRITE (2 sentences): the proportion lable is what i was trying to change but couldn’t figure it out.

A2 · Choose a scale

a2 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
 a2 <- fairness %>%
   filter(income > 0) %>%
   ggplot(aes(x = income)) +
   geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
   scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
   labs(title = "Income Graph", x = "Income (units, log scale)", y = "Count")

# YOUR TURN: one sentence. Why this scale for this column?
a2_reason <- "The majority of people make under 50k so a log scale helps spread those incomes out."

show_plot(a2)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): I chose a logarithmic scale because the majority of nc residents made less than 50k so using a log scale spreads those income values put.

A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

# YOUR TURN 1: replace "replace me" with your second column (no quotes).
a3_rates <- a_data %>%
  mutate(panel = sex) %>%
  drop_na(group) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = n / first(panel_n), .groups = "drop")
#adjusted summarize so that the graph properly shows above and below 50k income proportions

a3_fixed <- NULL
a3_free <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
 a3_fixed <- ggplot(a3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
   geom_col() +
   facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
   scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
   labs(title = "Gender and Income", x = "Gender", y = "Rate of income (%)")
 a3_free <- a3_fixed +
   facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")

# YOUR TURN 3: which one would you publish, "fixed" or "free_y"? Why?
a3_choice <- "fixed"
a3_reason <- "fixed scales keep the two panels proportionate to the total so its easier at a glance to see how they compare."

show_plot(a3_fixed)
show_plot(a3_free)

WRITE (3–4 sentences):Fixed because it keeps the scale between the male and female panels the same which lets viewers compare the rates across the panels easier. ### A4 · Compared to what?

Since there were now fewer categories the color check passed. ## Part B · Sports

B1 · Label it

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = period,
    has_outcome = period == 3,
    value = period_seconds_remaining
  )

b1_base <- b_data %>%
  count(has_outcome) %>%
  mutate(rate = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = has_outcome)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    x = "Share of total shots",
    y = "Period 3",
    fill = "Period"
  )

b1 <- b1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Share of shots in Period 3",
    subtitle = "Shows percentage of shots that happened in period 3",
    x = "Percentage",
    y = "True is Period 3"
  )

show_plot(b1)

WRITE (2 sentences): The plot shows the percentage of shots that occured in period 3. the most helpful lable is the y axis label.

B2 · Choose a scale

b2 <- NULL
b2 <- sports %>%
  filter(period > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = period)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Scaled Shots graph", x = "Shots (log scale)", y = "Count")


b2_reason <- "I dont know how much a log scale will do, there are only 6 values in the shots column (1-6)"

show_plot(b2)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): I chose a logarithmic scale because thats what I did for a3. It shows a standart count of how many shots occured in each period but it is spaced out odd due to the logarithmic scale.

B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

b3_rates <- b_data %>%
  mutate(panel = shot_outcome) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = n / first(panel_n), .groups = "drop")

b3_fixed <- ggplot(b3_rates, aes(x = factor(group), y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Shot Outcome by Period",
    x = "Period",
    y = "Rate of shots (%)"
  )

b3_free <- b3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")


b3_choice <- "fixed"
b3_reason <- "The two graphs look identical to me and i used fixed for a3"

show_plot(b3_fixed)
show_plot(b3_free)

WRITE (3–4 sentences): Fixed or free? What does the reader gain, and what do they lose? Which panels are small, and what is their n? Differences, not causes. Fixed scale because it allows for easier comparisons across the panels. They lose the ability to have a scale that best fits each panel but we gain the ability to more easily compare each panel.

B4 · Compared to what?

b4_clouds <- b_data %>%
  filter(shot_outcome %in% c("GOAL", "SHOT")) %>%
  make_clouds(shot_outcome, shot_distance)

b4 <- ggplot(b4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(
    title = "Shot Distance by Outcome, Resampled",
    x = "Shot Outcome",
    y = "Shot Distance (ft)"
  )

show_plot(b4)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): The clouds overlap heavily. the closer the shot was to the goal. Meaning that the closer the shot happened to the goal the more likely it was to score. ### B5 · Color for every reader

b5 <- b_data %>%
  mutate(period = fct_lump_n(as.factor(period), n = 3)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = period, fill = period)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Period Shots",
    x = "Count",
    y = "Period",
    fill = "Period"
  )

show_plot(b5)
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(b5)
4 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;

WRITE (2–4 sentences): My colors are greens and blues and the color is dictated by period. If each period was shown, the color check failed. So, I had to combine period 4, 5, and 6 into one group so that the color check passed. Periods 4, 5, and 6 were the smalled catagories by far.
